title: Is it the Buddha's word?
hookLine: Mahayana sees its sutras as the Buddha's teaching; many Theravada scholars see them as later; both views held in good faith
last: WHERE THE SUTRA IS OPENED, A SHRINE.

cards: Two monks share a train compartment. One wears the deep red of Tibet, the other the saffron of Sri Lanka. They get talking, and it's friendly, until one of them mentions the Heart Sutra.
The other smiles, a little carefully. In his monastery, that sutra isn't part of the canon. To him it's a beautiful later text.
To his neighbor, it's the Buddha's word. Neither raises his voice. Neither gets off at the next stop.

teach.b: First, what the Mahayana sutras say. They open the way the old discourses do: thus have I heard. The Buddha is there, the monks are there, a question is asked.
Mahayana communities receive these sutras as the Buddha's own teaching.
Some explain why they surfaced later with a story: tradition says certain sutras were kept safe by the nagas, serpent beings beneath the sea, until someone ready could bring them back.
Nagarjuna, the story goes, was that someone. Second, the Theravada view.

Theravada keeps the canon in Pali, and the Mahayana sutras aren't in it. There they're read as later works, written after the Buddha's lifetime, sometimes admired, not counted as his words. That's not a sneer.
It's a careful view about where a text came from.
Third, both sides already had a test.

In the Pali Great Passing discourse, the Buddha tells the monks what to do if someone claims, I heard this from the Lord himself: don't accept it and don't reject it; set it beside the discourses and the discipline, and see whether it fits.

Some Mahayana writers offered another measure: whatever is well spoken, whatever leads to freedom from suffering, carries the Buddha's word. Fourth, holding it. This path won't settle the question, and doesn't need to.
Mahayana Buddhists read their sutras in good faith. Theravada Buddhists keep their canon in good faith.
Both views are old, both are argued with care, and both belong to people who bow to the same Buddha.
What helps is the skill the monks on the train showed: to hear a view you don't hold all the way to the end, without rushing to win.

how: Mahayana Buddhists study and chant their sutras as the Buddha's teaching; Theravada Buddhists keep the Pali canon as the record of his words, and the two traditions meet and talk across this difference.

games.q: what does “is it the buddha's word?” mean?
o: a debate over which language the Buddha spoke at home
a test of whether a monk has memorized the canon correctly
an old question: are the Mahayana sutras the Buddha's teaching?

games.q: both held in good faith: tap the pairs.
p: a Mahayana measure of the word

s: the Mahayana sutras are part of the Pali canon
Theravada's Pali canon doesn't include them; in that tradition they're read as later works.
in the Pali canon the Buddha says to check a claimed teaching against the discourses
in the Great Passing discourse: don't accept or reject it at once; see whether it fits.
calling a sutra later is an insult in Theravada
it's a careful view about where a text came from, and some later texts are admired.

games.q: a monk tells you, 'I heard this teaching from the Buddha himself.' in the Pali canon, what does the Buddha say to do?
o: set it beside the discourses and see if it fits
games.why: neither accept nor reject at once. compare it with the discourses and the discipline. careful listening is built into the canon itself.

practice: Bring to mind a question where people you respect disagree, a family decision, a passage of scripture, the right way to do a thing.
Let one side speak in your mind in its best, kindest voice, then let the other side speak just as kindly. Don't pick; if you lean, notice the lean, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Is it the Buddha's word? Mahayana receives its sutras as his teaching; Theravada reads them as later. Two views, held side by side, ranked by no one here. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the word of the Buddha, what each school asks of its texts.

carryVoice: Your line: both held in good faith. Two tests, one teacher. Tomorrow, the turn, closed.
